content: 1. Rnande et al. (2013): This study investigates the relationship between early-life weight and weight gain as predictors of obesity in Brazilian adolescents. The findings highlight the importance of monitoring weight trajectories in early life to mitigate the risk of adolescent obesity. 2. Biro et al. (2010): The research explores how childhood body mass index (BMI) influences changes in BMI and waist-to-height ratio during adolescence in girls. The study underscores the long-term impact of childhood BMI on adolescent body composition. 3. Burns et al. (2011): This study identifies childhood predictors of metabolic syndrome in middle-aged adults, using data from the Muscatine study. It emphasizes the significance of early-life health metrics in forecasting adult metabolic health. 4. Angbratt et al. (2011): The authors examine the prediction of obesity from infancy to adolescence, demonstrating the critical role of early growth patterns in determining later obesity risk. 5. Casey et al. (2012): This research tracks the evolution of obesity in a cohort of low birth weight individuals, revealing the long-term implications of birth weight on obesity development. 6. Chen et al. (2011): A longitudinal study from the Da Qing children cohort investigates childhood adiposity and its association with the risk of developing components of metabolic syndrome, highlighting the importance of early adiposity management. 7. Al Mamun et al. (2009): This follow-up study shows that childhood overweight status is a strong predictor of diabetes at age 21, emphasizing the need for early interventions to prevent long-term metabolic disorders. 8. Chen et al. (2010): The Bogalusa Heart Study demonstrates that the association between birth weight and blood pressure amplifies with age, suggesting that early-life factors have a cumulative effect on cardiovascular health. 9. Chen et al. (2011): This study links childhood blood pressure variability to adult hypertension in both Black and White populations, based on data from the Bogalusa Heart Study. 10. Sachdev et al. (2009): The New Delhi Birth Cohort study highlights the predictive value of childhood BMI for adult metabolic syndrome, emphasizing the need for early-life interventions. 11. Fonseca et al. (2010): The Rio de Janeiro study examines the relationship between overweight status and cardiovascular risk among young adults over a 17-year follow-up period. 12. Gordon-Larsen et al. (2010): This study tracks longitudinal trends in obesity from adolescence to the third decade of life in the United States, providing insights into the progression of obesity over time. 13. González et al. (2010): The authors explore the relationship between growth from birth to adulthood and abdominal obesity in a Brazilian birth cohort, emphasizing the role of early growth patterns in determining adult adiposity. 14. Chen et al. (2007): The Bogalusa Heart Study identifies clustering of long-term trends in metabolic syndrome variables from childhood to adulthood, highlighting racial differences in these patterns. 15. Baker et al. (2007): This study links childhood BMI to the risk of coronary heart disease in adulthood, underscoring the long-term cardiovascular implications of early-life obesity. 16. Frohner et al. (2013): The authors investigate the relationship between serum free fatty acids, adiposity, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular risk factors from adolescence to adulthood. 17. Barker et al. (2005): This study examines growth trajectories in children who experience coronary events as adults, emphasizing the importance of early growth monitoring. 18. Bhargava et al. (2004): The New Delhi Birth Cohort study links serial changes in childhood BMI to impaired glucose tolerance in young adulthood. 19. Cooper et al. (2009): Evidence from the 1958 British birth cohort shows that gestational age is associated with cardiovascular risk factors in mid-life. 20. Craigie et al. (2009): This longitudinal study demonstrates that elevated adolescent BMI predicts adult adiposity and central fat distribution. 21. Freedman et al. (2005): The Bogalusa Heart Study highlights the relationship between childhood BMI and adult adiposity, emphasizing the importance of early BMI tracking. 22. Deshmukh-Taskar et al. (2006): This study tracks overweight status from childhood to young adulthood, providing insights into the persistence of obesity over time. 23. Fall et al. (2008): Data from the New Delhi Birth Cohort show that different patterns of BMI gain during infancy are associated with adult metabolic syndrome and impaired glucose tolerance. 24. Wheeler (2013): A community-based cohort study identifies the risk of obesity at ages 4 to 6 among overweight or obese 18-month-olds. 25. Williams and Goulding (2008): This study examines growth patterns associated with the timing of adiposity rebound, highlighting its implications for later obesity risk. 26. Wells et al. (2012): A Brazilian birth cohort study investigates the associations of intrauterine and postnatal weight and length gains with adolescent body composition. 27. Wright et al. (2012): The Gateshead Millennium Study explores the extent to which weight gain and eating avidity during infancy predict later adiposity. 28. Willers et al. (2012): The PIAMA study examines BMI development in normal weight and overweight children, providing insights into early-life predictors of obesity. 29. Wright et al. (2010): This study tracks obesity and body fatness through mid-childhood, emphasizing the importance of early monitoring. 30. Ziyab et al. (2014): The authors investigate developmental trajectories of BMI from infancy to 18 years, focusing on prenatal determinants and health consequences. 31. Wang et al. (2000): A six-year follow-up study in China tracks BMI from childhood to adolescence, highlighting the persistence of BMI trends. 32. Wardle et al. (2006): A five-year longitudinal study in Britain examines the development of adiposity in adolescence, considering ethnic and socioeconomic diversity. 33. White and Jago (2013): This study explores the relationship between fat distribution, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk among adolescent girls. 34. Wang et al. (2008): The authors investigate the association between adolescent BMI and adult obesity, emphasizing the importance of early BMI management. 35. Burke et al. (2005): A prospective cohort study in Australia identifies predictors of BMI and their associations with cardiovascular risk factors in children. 36. Belfort et al. (2007): This study examines the relationship between size at birth, infant growth, and blood pressure at three years of age. 37. Frontini et al. (2004): The Bogalusa Heart Study investigates the longitudinal trends of cardiovascular risk factors from childhood to adolescence in low birth weight individuals. 38. Gardner et al. (2009): The EarlyBird 36 study examines the contribution of early weight gain to childhood overweight and metabolic health. 39. Drozdz et al. (2009): This study explores the correlation between fat mass and blood pressure in healthy children. 40. Gaskin and Walker (2003): A cohort study in Jamaica estimates obesity using BMI and other indices of adiposity in Black children. 41. Dennison et al. (2006): Rapid infant weight gain is identified as a predictor of childhood overweight, emphasizing the need for early growth monitoring. 42. Ekelund et al. (2006): The Stockholm Weight Development Study shows that upward weight percentile crossing in infancy predicts fat mass in young adults. 43. Crimmins et al. (2007): This study examines the stability of adolescent BMI over three years of follow-up. 44. Finucane et al. (2008): A cohort of obese Irish children is studied to identify adverse metabolic profiles. 45. Beltrand et al. (2012): Post-term birth is associated with a greater risk of obesity in adolescent males. 46. Heys et al. (2013): The Children of 1997 birth cohort in Hong Kong investigates lifetime growth and blood pressure in adolescence. 47. Cunningham et al. (2014): This study examines the incidence of childhood obesity in the United States. 48. Lawlor et al. (2010): A prospective cohort study investigates the association between general and central adiposity in childhood and cardiovascular risk factors in adolescence. 49. Reilly et al. (2005): The Avon Longitudinal Study identifies early-life risk factors for childhood obesity. 50. Ong et al. (2000): Postnatal catch-up growth is associated with childhood obesity, as shown in a prospective cohort study. 51. Reilly et al. (2011): This study examines the progression from childhood overweight to adolescent obesity in a contemporary cohort. 52. Power and Thomas (2011): A 45-year follow-up of a birth cohort investigates changes in BMI, duration of overweight, and glucose metabolism. 53. Pinto Pereira and Power (2013): A nationwide birth cohort study links life course BMI and birth weight to lipid levels in mid-adulthood. 54. Power et al. (1997): The 1958 British birth cohort study examines BMI and height from childhood to adulthood. 55. Park et al. (2013): A pooled analysis of three British birth cohorts investigates the relationship between overweight in childhood, adolescence, and adulthood with cardiovascular risk in later life. 56. Laitinen et al. (2004): Predictors of abdominal obesity among 31-year-old men and women born in Northern Finland in 1966 are identified. 57. Sovio et al. (2014): The Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 study examines how changes in BMI in infancy and childhood associate with cardiometabolic profiles in adulthood. 58. Tzoulaki et al. (2010): Immediate postnatal growth is linked to obesity and related metabolic risk factors in adulthood, as shown in the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 study. 59. Thiering et al. (2012): Peak growth velocity in infancy is positively associated with blood pressure in school-aged children. 60. Pei et al. (2013): Early-life risk factors for being overweight at 10 years of age are identified in the German birth cohorts GINIplus and LISAplus. 61. Srinivasan et al. (2006): Childhood non-HDL cholesterol levels are predictive of adult dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risks, as shown in the Bogalusa Heart Study. 62. Srinivasan et al. (2006): Changes in metabolic syndrome variables since childhood are examined in prehypertensive and hypertensive subjects in the Bogalusa Heart Study. 63. Wadsworth et al. (2005): Evidence from the 1946 British birth cohort links early growth to type 2 diabetes risk. 64. Law et al. (2002): A longitudinal study from birth to 22 years of age examines the relationship between fetal, infant, and childhood growth and adult blood pressure. 65. Odegaard et al. (2013): A systematic examination of infant size and growth metrics identifies risk factors for overweight in young adulthood. 66. Raitakari et al. (2005): The Cardiovascular Risk in Young Finns Study investigates the relationship between childhood obesity and vascular changes in adulthood. 67. Raitakari et al. (2005): Cardiovascular risk factors in childhood are associated with carotid artery intima-media thickness in adulthood, as shown in the Cardiovascular Risk in Young Finns Study.
